doc.title: Cedar Walton — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

chapter: Dallas childhood, training and early playing
title: Dallas modern jazz underground; rhythm and blues on the bandstand
summary: Walton says the rhythm was simplified for audiences and everything was rhythm and blues, but at fifteen or sixteen he was glad to be on any bandstand.

story.theme_name: First paying gigs: getting started as a young professional
story.community_name: First paid gigs: pay, bands and young beginnings

blocks.x: So, I'm trying to, um, I guess, the picture I’m getting about Dallas in your youth was … there was, to the extent that the modern jazz thing was happening, was more or less underground.
And, you know, the music you were playing out … was jazz but not …
It had the undercurrent of uh, the, the, the, uh …

No, the rhythm was uh, made simple, so to speak, you know, condescending in a way to the listeners. Well, in the sense to me when I think about it now. You know, I mean there just … we had to simplify. We can't play like we know it, that it could be very enjoyable here because people will start talking or it would be uh, uh, uh, unfamiliar to them, you know. That's where, that's …
Are you saying Rhythm & Blues too?
That's what I'm talkin' about. Everything was Rhythm & Blues, instrumentally. And then somebody would inevitably sing too. But uh …
Did you enjoy that at all, or …
Yeah! Yeah, I was just glad to be on any bandstand. Yeah, I was very young still – 15 or you know, 16, thereabouts. So uh …
